extracted.intended_audience: educational psychologists, instructional designers, multimedia learning researchers, and educators interested in cognitive load theory and instructional design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principled effects from cognitive load theory for designing instruction, multimedia, and curriculum (including 4C/ID). Emphasises principles, named effects, and component-based design recommendations for managing working memory and promoting learning/transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation of diagram + auditory/spoken text (audio) is more effective than diagram + integrated written text (visual). Effective working memory capacity can be increased by using both visual and auditory working memory rather than either processor alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If split-attention occurs, presenting written information in an auditory mode may be equally or more effective than physically integrating it into the diagram. See Mousavi et al. (1995) and Ginns (2005a) meta-analysis. Beware interactions with transient information (long audio may be harmful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Variability across problem situations encourages construction of more general knowledge and increases probability of identifying relevant features; increases intrinsic cognitive load but can increase transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High variability benefits learning/transfer when cognitive load is low (e.g. learning from worked examples) but can harm learning when cognitive load is already high (e.g. conventional problem solving). Design should lower extraneous load first; then increasing germane load via variability is beneficial provided total cognitive load stays within limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce extraneous before increasing germane load
rubrics_metrics.description: When instruction is designed, it should first decrease extraneous cognitive load, but instructional designs effective at decreasing extraneous load may be even more effective if they increase germane processing, provided total cognitive load remains within limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance reductions in extraneous load with deliberate increases in germane load (e.g. through variability, prompts) only when working memory capacity is not exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biologically primary vs secondary knowledge distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Biologically primary knowledge (evolved, acquired effortlessly, modular/generic-cognitive) vs biologically secondary knowledge (cultural, domain-specific, requires conscious effort and explicit instruction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary knowledge should be taught explicitly; attempts to teach purely generic-cognitive (primary) skills for far transfer tend to fail. Use primary skills to assist teaching secondary skills (e.g. point out when to apply a generic skill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Store Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Human cognition requires a large store of information provided by long-term memory; long-term memory functions as a biologically primary information store.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction can rely on building and using long-term memory structures; designing for retrieval from LTM reduces working memory demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borrowing and Reorganising Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Most information in long-term memory is obtained from others; humans evolved procedures for obtaining and providing information socially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional design should capitalise on social transmission (explicit instruction) rather than forcing learners to generate information themselves when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomness as Genesis Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When information is unavailable, novel information is generated via random generate-and-test during problem solving; this is biologically primary and does not require instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on learners to generate domain-specific knowledge via random search is inefficient; provide supportive instruction when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow Limits of Change Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Working memory has severe limitations when processing novel information; general working memory capacity is limited and can vary (e.g. depletion and recovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction to manage element interactivity and avoid overloading working memory; consider rest/recovery effects on capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental Organising and Linking Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Once information is organised in long-term memory, environmental cues can trigger appropriate actions; organised LTM removes working memory limits for familiar information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to construct organized LTM schemas so learners can retrieve and apply knowledge with low working memory cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4C/ID component: Learning tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning tasks are preferably real-life tasks that let learners acquire non-recurrent and recurrent constituent skills; tasks are organised by increasing complexity (a spiral curriculum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage intrinsic cognitive load by sequencing tasks from simple to complex; decrease learner support as complexity increases; include high variability across tasks to stimulate germane processing; use completion strategy (worked examples → completion tasks → conventional tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4C/ID component: Supportive information
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive information helps learners with non-recurrent aspects (problem solving, reasoning) and explains domain organisation ('theory'); it typically has high element interactivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present supportive information before learners start the learning task or apart from task work to avoid cognitive overload; connect supportive information to task complexity and prior knowledge; use it to build knowledge structures in LTM that can be retrieved during task performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4C/ID component: Procedural information
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural information consists of just-in-time 'how-to' instructions and corrective feedback for recurrent aspects; it has lower element interactivity than supportive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present procedural information precisely when learners need it during task performance (assistant-over-the-shoulder style) to support rule formation and automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4C/ID component: Part-task practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Part-task practice targets selected recurrent task aspects to strengthen automation (cognitive rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use part-task practice sparingly—automate basic/critical recurrent skills when useful (e.g. arithmetic facts, instrument operation) to free working memory for non-recurrent aspects; avoid over-reliance on part-task practice for complex skill learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion strategy (fading-guidance approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fading-guidance approach where learners move from studying worked examples through completion tasks to conventional problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use completion strategy as a practical method of guidance fading: start with worked examples, then require learners to complete parts of solutions, then full problem solving as expertise grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element interactivity effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Element interactivity modifies other cognitive load effects: effects obtained using high element interactivity materials can disappear or reverse with low element interactivity materials (and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify material element interactivity or consider learner expertise when applying instructional effects; examples show conventional worked example effects may reverse with low-interactivity material such as definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise reversal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional procedures beneficial for novices (high element interactivity) can become redundant or counterproductive as learners gain expertise because interacting elements become chunked in LTM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt instruction as expertise increases: worked examples help novices, whereas practice/problem solving becomes more important for more knowledgeable learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance-fading effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance or additional instructional support should be faded as learners gain expertise; what is essential for novices may become redundant and impose unnecessary load on more expert learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop long-duration programs with gradually decreasing support; examples include completion strategy and other fading methods discussed by Renkl and van Merriënboer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transient information effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Transient information (e.g. spoken text, animations) that disappears after a few seconds increases extraneous cognitive load because learners must actively retain it in working memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate transient-information effects using self-pacing, segmentation (segmented animations with pauses), or other compensatory strategies. Note interaction with modality: short audio-visual segments can be beneficial, but longer audio-visual segments may be less effective than visual-only presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-management effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Students can be taught to apply cognitive load theory principles themselves to manage their own cognitive load when confronted with poorly designed materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction that teaches learners to reorganise split-attention materials (self-management training) can yield superior recall and transfer compared to instructor-managed physical integration; studies typically use phases comparing self-management, split-attention, and physically integrated conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-explanation effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Worked examples combined with self-explanation prompts elicit deeper processing and can be superior to worked examples alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide self-explanation prompts especially when only a single example is available; ensure total cognitive load (including germane load from self-explanation) does not exceed working memory capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking learners to mentally rehearse or imagine concepts/processes can improve learning relative to study instructions, provided learners can adequately imagine the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novices may be unable to imagine high element-interactivity material (so study > imagination); with increased knowledge, imagination instructions can become superior to study. Use imagination when learners have sufficient prior knowledge to process imagined information in working memory.
